catalog_quote: Puxi distinguishes a simple tone system with two contrastive tones, high and low. High and low tones are normally realized by high-falling pitch and low-rising pitch respectively, as seen in these tonally differentiated pairs: ... The pitch patterns in words containing more than one syllable are conspicuously limited, owing to an interlocking system of accent. In fact, the two-way tonal contrast can be carried only by the accented syllable in a polysyllabic word. Accent, borne potentially by any of the last three syllables of a word, is henceforth represented by the acute accent @; since final accent is by far the most common accent position, it can be regarded as a default and left unmarked. new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (22 pp., text layer present; extraction alongside). Sec. 1.2.2 'Tonality' sits on journal p. 216 exactly as located. The quoted passage is there; the only departures are dropped footnote callouts (7, 8) and the dropped acute-accent glyph (rendered '@' in the text layer: 'represented by the acute accent @;'), with the ellipses correctly marking the skipped example sets (5)-(6) and the clause 'phonetically distinct from the low tone'. Surrounding text read in full (secs. 1.1, 1.2, 2.2, 3.1.1): Sun states two contrastive tones (H = [53], L = [13]) on monosyllables; in polysyllables the contrast is carried only by one accented syllable, which may be any of the last three syllables…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Each word has one accented syllable within a final three-syllable window (final, penult or antepenult), lexically/morphologically determined but final by default (most common); only the accented syllable bears the H (falling) vs L (rising) tone contrast; post-accent syllables are low-level, pre-accent syllables mid. In verb morphology certain orientation/aspect prefixes obligatorily attract the accent in high-toned non-negated forms, and some prefixed high-tone verbs take penultimate accent; low-toned disyllabic verbs are always final-accented.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; non-accented syllables get predictable pitch (mid before, low-level after the accent).
new_statements.exceptions: Accent position is not fully predictable: antepenult and penult accent occur lexically (e.g. 'sparrow', 'earthworm' with antepenult accent); orientation prefixes n´- 'downward', g´- 'westward', ld´- 'upstream' obligatorily take accent in high-toned non-negated verb forms while other prefixes never do; high-tone polysyllabic verbs with 'eastward'/'downstream' prefixes are penult-accented; derived past stems always final-accented on the low-toned syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent (citation forms and inflected verb words); Sun explicitly likens it to Baltic/South Slavic 'partial word tones' (fn. 8) and calls it a pitch accent system. Data from one hamlet of Puxi Village (fieldwork 1995-1999).
new_statements.identity_note: Sun 2000 describes the Puxi (phosi) variety of Shangzhai = Stodsde (shan1274), speech of one hamlet of Puxi Village, Puxi Township, Rangtang (Ndzamthang) County; Sun treats Shangzhai and Horpa as dialects of one 'Horpa-Shangzhai' language but the data and the prosodic statement are specifically Puxi Shangzhai, i.e. shan1274 proper, not Stau/Geshiza Horpa (horp1239 etc.), which Sun and Jacques et al. report as lacking tone/contrastive accent.

sources.locator: sec. 1.2.2 'Tonality', p. 216 (with fn. 8); cf. sec. 2, pp. 220-221, fn. 15
sources.note: Sec. 1.2.2 'Tonality' (p.216): two contrastive tones (H falling / L rising) carried only by the accented syllable of a polysyllable; accent may fall on any of the last three syllables, final accent 'by far the most common' and treated as default/unmarked; post-accent syllables predictable low-level, pre-accent syllables mid ('pitch accent system'). Sec. 2 adds morphological accent shifts: certain orientation/aspect prefixes obligatorily attract accent in high-toned non-negated verb forms; low-toned disyllabic verbs always final-accented (fn.15).
